items.title: [kmac/doc] Correct peak performance numbers of Keccak core
items.body:
When updating these figures in b968a168c2faf600c0174b5328bfabe8ffca036c, I erroneously assumed that the padding was added to every block instead of just the last block of a message.

So it really takes `block size / 64` clock cycles to load the data into the Keccak core (rather than a flat 25 clock cycles) and then either 24 or 96 clock cycles for the processing of the 24 Keccak rounds.

This results in 144 (SHA3-224) or 72 bytes (SHA3-512) being processed every 42 or 33 (unmasked), or every 114 or 105 clock cycles (masked).

items.title: docs: use Task Manager's memory metric, verified across repeated runs
items.body:
Follow-up to #295, which corrected the performance numbers but used the wrong memory metric to do it. This fixes the metric and verifies the result across repeated runs.

## The error

I was summing each process's **total working set** across the process tree. That double-counts pages shared between processes, so it inflates a seven-process WebView2 app against a single-process native one. Chromium rejects the same metric for the same reason:

> "We couldn't use the Total Working Set, because this measure double-counts the shared memory used by each process."

Task Manager's **Memory** column is *active private working set*, which for plain Win32 processes equals private working set. In PowerShell that is `Win32_PerfRawData_PerfProc_Process.WorkingSetPrivate` — verified to be the same counter as `\Process(x)\Working Set - Private`, and a `PERF_COUNTER_LARGE_RAWCOUNT`, so a single read is valid with no two-sample formula.

It is also the only figure a reader can reproduce by opening Task Manager, which is why it belongs in a README over Chromium's own PrivateMemoryFootprint (private commit).

## Measured

Release builds, same machine, same 119-addon profile, 100 s settle, repeated cold launches, summed across the process tree:

| | Samples (MB) | Median |
|---|---|---|
| Webview, window open | 132, 133, 136, 137, 139, 142, 148 | **137** |
| Webview, minimized | 14, 18, 19 | **18** |
| Slint, window open | 81, 82, 83, 86, 90 | **83** |

Two readings during an interleaved A/B pass came in at 154 and 206 MB for the webview. Five clean trials immediately afterwards landed 132–139, so those reflect system memory pressure during that pass rather than the app.

## This closes the open question from #295

I flagged there that the beta.10 changelog's "~142 MB" might be a regression, since I was measuring 436 MB. It is not. 142 sits inside the measured range and reproduces today. The changelog was right; I was comparing against a metric that counts shared pages once per process.

## Wording

Native is now "~85 MB from around 135 MB" rather than the "130 against 440" the bad metric implied — about 40% less, not the "roughly half" I claimed in #295, and nowhere near the 3x the total-working-set sum suggested.

The minimized figure is stated as "under 20 MB" rather than a precise number. It reproduces, but it is resident memory only: suspending trims the working set without releasing the commitment, which stays at 337–502 MB. A precise number there would imply more than the measurement supports.

items.title: fix(bench-gate): the H1 directive gate can be cleared by a one-token lookup table
items.body:
Closes #1341.

The H1 bench gate was never re-run after the fix it was waiting on shipped. Re-running it turned up a stale published number, and then a larger problem: the gate cannot certify what it claims to certify.

## 1. The published number was stale

`docs/design/v2_directive_detection.md` and `docs/design/V2_REENTRY_QUEUE.md` have both carried **P=0.664** since May. That is the *pre*-Path-A figure. Path A shipped in #467 and the confirming re-run the memo itself asked for ("needs corpus re-run to confirm") never happened.

Measured against the shipped detector, lab corpus v0.1, 285 rows:

```
precision 0.706 below 0.8 gate (TP=89, FP=37, FN=6, TN=153, n=285)
```

**P=0.706 / R=0.937.** Path A removed **8** false positives, not the ~45 estimated — off by about 5x. And the surviving errors are not the "single dominant pattern" the failure analysis described; they fall into six structurally distinct families (interrogatives the filters miss, attribution, third-person descriptive, use/mention, task verbs outside the prefix bank, and stance/affirmation frames).

## 2. The gate can be cleared by a one-token lookup table

This is the finding that matters, and it is why this PR ships no detector change.

Partition the corpus deterministically, 163 train / 122 held out. Build the weakest classifier that can be written: read the **first word** of the prompt, look up the majority label for that word among training rows, answer with it. No grammar, no mood, no notion of durability or task-versus-rule.

```
held out:  P=0.912  R=0.795   (TP=31, FP=3, FN=8)   -> clears P>=0.80 / R>=0.60
```

It clears the gate. The real detector scores 0.706 and does not.

The cause is in the corpus. Of 114 distinct opening words, only **7** appear in both classes — 87.9% of rows are decided by their first token. Positives open with deontic/policy vocabulary (`always`, `never`, `don't`, `avoid`, `prefer`, `use`); negatives open with task, question and discourse vocabulary (`write`, `run`, `check`, `what`, `should`, `ok`, `please`). **No row labelled `directive` opens with a one-shot task verb.**

So any rule keyed on head position buys precision for free. It is never charged for the durable directives it would wrongly suppress, because the corpus contains none of them — no "Check every PR for a changelog entry before you approve it", no "Run the full suite before pushing to a shared branch". Those are ordinary standing rules that open with a task verb, and a head-verb filter eats them in production while scoring clean in-corpus.

## 3. How that was established, and what did not ship

Six family-scoped suppression rules were built against the **train split only**, each self-measured, then each put through independent adversarial review. Composed, they took the corpus to **P=0.953 / R=0.853** — a comfortable pass, and it held up on the held-out split (P=0.944).

Every one of the six was judged both overfit and over-reaching, unanimously, with concrete minimal pairs. Representative: a rule claiming to detect interrogative force by subject-auxiliary inversion actually keyed on a closed pronoun list — `should we only run the migration on Postgres` is suppressed, `should the migration only run on the Postgres shard` is not, identical syntax. Another suppressed genuine directives outright: `Check each incoming PR for a changelog entry before you approve it`.

**None of them are in this PR.** The one-token baseline explains why they measured so well and reviewed so badly, and a gate that a lookup table passes will bless an overfit detector — it nearly did here.

## What this PR contains

- `test_directive_corpus_defeats_a_first_token_baseline` — a bench-gate guard that trains the baseline on whatever corpus is mounted and fails if it clears the gate. A statement about the corpus, not the detector. **Red against v0.1 by design**; skips in public CI with the rest of the bench gate.
- The corrected numbers in both design docs, the six-family failure analysis replacing the monolithic-cluster one, a § Gate validity recording the measurement, and corpus v0.2 made the blocking item ahead of further detector iteration.
- Changelog entry.

No change to `src/`. Detector behaviour is byte-identical.

## Verification

```
# public CI posture (corpus unset)
$ pytest -q tests/bench_gate/test_directive_detection.py
2 skipped

# lab, corpus mounted
$ AELFRICE_CORPUS_ROOT=... pytest -q tests/bench_gate/test_directive_detection.py
FAILED test_directive_detection_gate            - precision 0.706 below 0.8
FAILED test_directive_corpus_defeats_a_first_token_baseline
        - a first-token-only classifier clears the H1 gate on held-out rows
          (P=0.912, R=0.795, TP=31, FP=3, FN=8, train=163, held_out=122)
```

Both reds are the intended state against v0.1 and both are invisible to public CI.

## What this unblocks, and what it does not

#1315 (natural-language capture for time-boxed locks) is blocked on "H1 gate met, or a narrower detector proposed with its own gate". This PR does not clear that blocker — it establishes that clearing it against v0.1 would have meant nothing. The path is corpus v0.2: minimal pairs that break the head-word/class correlation, hard positives (durable rules opening with task verbs, absent today) and hard negatives (one-shot requests opening with policy verbs). Target: class-ambiguous opening words rise from 12.1% to a majority.

Corpus rows stay lab-side throughout. Only aggregate statistics cross the boundary.

Two lab-side corpus-hygiene notes, neither blocking: the label vocabulary is `not-directive` while `tests/corpus/v2_0/README.md` documents `not_directive`, and the `provenance` field the same README requires to be non-empty is absent from all 285 rows.

## Summary by Sourcery

Add a corpus-validity guard for the H1 directive-detection bench gate and correct related documentation and changelog entries.

New Features:
- Introduce a bench-gate test that ensures the directive-detection corpus cannot be solved by a first-token-only baseline classifier before treating gate metrics as evidence.

Bug Fixes:
- Clarify via changelog and design docs that the directive-detection bench gate could be spuriously cleared by a one-token lookup table and record the fix as a corpus-level guard rather than a detector change.

Enhancements:
- Document that the existing directive-detection gate is currently invalid due to corpus issues and outline requirements for corpus v0.2 before further detector iteration.
- Update design and re-entry-queue docs with corrected precision/recall figures and an expanded failure-mode analysis for the directive detector.

Documentation:
- Augment directive-detection design docs with a gate-validity section, corrected performance numbers, and guidance on corpus v0.2, and update the v2 re-entry queue accordingly.

Tests:
- Add a bench-gated test that fails when a first-token-only classifier clears the directive-detection H1 gate, treating this as a corpus problem rather than a detector issue.

Chores:
- Record the updated directive-detection status and gate conditions in the v4 changelog.

items.title: ⚡ Bolt: Hoist extension sorting outside initialization loop
items.body:
**💡 What:** Hoisted the sorting logic for `enabled_exts` outside the `while True` loop in `ExtensionManager._try_initialize_available`.

**🎯 Why:** Re-sorting the same `enabled_exts` list inside the `while` loop on every pass of the dependency resolution causes redundant `O(N log N)` overhead since `enabled_exts` itself is a static snapshot and its priority values do not mutate during initialization. Hoisting it provides `O(N log N)` computation just once.

**📊 Impact:** Prevents redundant `O(N log N)` sorting operations during application extension initialization, making app boot times faster, especially with high numbers of extensions.

**🔬 Measurement:** Execution tests show the same functional correctness, and performance profiles of boot operations over large numbers of extensions will reflect eliminated sort operations over multiple dependency resolution loop iterations.

items.body:
# EWB Pull Request

## Description

This is the part of #377 that is worth keeping, rebuilt on `develop` as two small
commits. #377 itself should be closed: an ablation showed its two headline
rewrites *are* the end-to-end regression, and that partial reverts of them break
correctness. See the addendum in the performance investigation write-up for the
numbers.

**Two correctness fixes that were buried in the perf PR.**

`maybe_densify_dataarray` assigned into the array it was handed:

```python
da.data = da.data.todense()   # mutates the parent Dataset's variable
```

Densifying one variable therefore mutated the dataset it came from, so unrelated
callers holding the same object observed a dense array where they expected a
sparse one. It now returns `da.copy(data=...)`.

`MaximumMeanAbsoluteError._compute_metric` hardcoded
`reduce_spatial_dims = ["latitude", "longitude"]`, silently ignoring whatever the
caller configured on the instance. Any non-default `reduce_spatial_dims` was
discarded.

items.title: perf(lsp): cache wildcard-reexport flag and precompute excluded-file set for auto-import
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes two hot paths in LSP auto-import candidate collection that were causing the top-10 fourslash slow tests to consume ~100s cumulative per CI run (issue #7590).

## Project Corpus Impact

- Row: n/a
- Bug family: LSP auto-import candidate collection performance for wildcard reexports and autoImportFileExcludePatterns
- Evidence: targets the #7590 top-10 fourslash slow-test family by moving wildcard-reexport detection and exclude-glob checks out of the per-symbol inner loop; full CI/fourslash performance gates remain CI-owned.

### Structural rule

> When N files are walked for M symbols with P exclude-glob patterns, glob evaluation must be O(N×P) per request, not O(N×M×P). Wildcard-reexport scanning must be O(1) per file per request, not O(statements) per file per request.

### Root causes

**Hot path 1 — `file_has_wildcard_reexport`**

Previously, every call walked the full statement list of a file to detect `export *`, `export { default }`, or `export = ` patterns. With N files and M symbols, this ran O(N×M×statements) per request. The function was called inside the per-symbol per-file loop in both `collect_import_candidates_for_name_with_mode` and `collect_import_candidates_for_prefix`.

Fix: compute `has_wildcard_reexport` once at `ProjectFile` construction time (in `with_shared_interner_and_file_idx`) and cache it as a `bool` field. `file_has_wildcard_reexport` becomes a single `HashMap` lookup — O(1) per call.

**Hot path 2 — `auto_import_path_is_excluded`**

This ran glob matching against all `auto_import_file_exclude_matchers` for every `(symbol, file)` pair inside the inner loop — O(N×M×P) total. The `autoImportFileExcludePatterns` fourslash tests that appear in the slow-test top-10 all exercise this path.

Fix: build an `excluded_file_set: FxHashSet<String>` once per request (before the per-symbol loop) in both collector functions, guarded by an early exit when `auto_import_file_exclude_matchers` is empty (the common case). The inner loop then does a O(1) `HashSet::contains` lookup. Total cost becomes O(N×P) per request regardless of M.

### Owning layer

- `has_wildcard_reexport` lives on `ProjectFile` (`project/core.rs`) — the right place because it is a structural property of a parsed file, computed once.
- `excluded_file_set` is local to each request in `project/imports.rs` — the right place because it is request-scoped (the file set can change between requests).

### Adjacent cases covered by the fix

1. `collect_import_candidates_for_name_with_mode` (single-symbol lookup)
2. `collect_import_candidates_for_prefix` (prefix/completion lookup)
3. Zero-exclude-pattern projects (fast path: empty set, zero extra work)
4. Files with only named re-exports (correctly `has_wildcard_reexport = false`)
5. Files with `export * from '...'` (correctly `has_wildcard_reexport = true`)
6. Files with `export { default } from '...'` (correctly `has_wildcard_reexport = true`)

### Test matrix

Two new regression tests in `crates/tsz-lsp/src/project/imports.rs`:

- `has_wildcard_reexport_cached_on_project_file`: verifies the cached field is computed correctly at `ProjectFile` construction for plain exports, named-only re-exports, `export *`, and `export { default }` patterns.
- `file_exclude_patterns_applied_once_per_request_not_per_symbol`: verifies that with an `**/excluded/**` pattern, symbols from an excluded package are absent from prefix-search results while symbols from an included package appear correctly.

### Performance numbers

The fourslash tests in the slow-test top-10 that exercise `autoImportFileExcludePatterns` (e.g. `fourslash/codeFixAddMissingImport_excludePatterns*.ts`) were identified in issue #7590 as consuming disproportionate time due to these two hot paths. The structural fix eliminates per-(symbol,file) glob re-evaluation entirely.

## Project Corpus Impact

Row: LSP / fourslash auto-import tests (`autoImportFileExcludePatterns` family)
Bug family: O(N×M×P) glob re-evaluation per auto-import request; O(statements) wildcard scan per (symbol, file)
Evidence: `cargo nextest run -p tsz_lsp` — 3801/3801 tests pass (net +2 new regression tests); issue #7590 identifies this as the top-10 fourslash slow-test root cause

items.title: fix(editor): close audit-confirmed defects in Epic #2096 governed debugging (DAP)
items.body:
## Summary

Post-merge production-readiness audit of **Epic #2096** (Built-in editor M8 — governed
Node.js/TypeScript debugging foundation, DAP) and all seven child issues **#2342–#2348**, which
shipped in #2398 (`feb6f478`). The epic and children were already merged and closed; this change
fixes the confirmed defects a deep, independent audit surfaced across the child issues, the
epic-level integration, and a production-readiness sweep (security, performance, accessibility,
maintainability), plus closes the mutation survivors the audit's own additions introduced.

The audit was run as a 23-agent workflow (7 per-child audits → per-child fix rounds → epic
integration audit → 4 production-readiness sweeps → fix rounds), with every fix verified by a
regression test that fails before the fix and passes after, then reconciled at the coordinator level.

## What was fixed

**Epic-level integration (found only when the children are combined):**

- **BLOCKER — the epic's flagship demo was unreachable.** Every UI Start/Continue call site built an
  unconditional `{ kind: "file" }` launch target, so the fully-implemented server-side
  catalog-derived launch path (#2344/#2345) had no caller. "Debug this test file" (the epic's own
  headline scenario, and the only way to debug a vitest test) could never run. Added a shared
  `resolveDebugLaunchTarget` seam that routes a recognized test file through the existing M4
  command-runner catalog and falls back to the file-target launch otherwise.
- **MAJOR — breakpoint gutter collided with the M5 git-gutter/blame decorations.** None of the three
  gutter bridges set Monaco's `glyphMargin.position`, so all decorations stacked on the default
  Center lane. Added a shared lane-assignment module and gave each bridge a distinct lane.

**Per-child fixes (highlights):**

- **#2343** — the no-post-launch-restart guard (ADR-0136 D5) was permanently dead (always called
  `mayStart(now, false)`); wired it to real launched state. Added a private-Unix-domain-socket
  handshake integration test proving the manager and a spawned fake adapter complete a real DAP
  exchange over the production transport.
- **#2344** — the ADR-0136 D4 "Layer-1 command-rule approval" step was a no-op duplicate of Layer-2;
  replaced it with a genuine, independent `isCommandAllowed`/`CommandRule` check that rejects
  dangerous node/npm flags in argv.
- **#2345** — breakpoint-store and activation-revalidation swallowed genuine disk/resolver failures
  with no diagnostic; routed them through the established redacted correlation-id diagnostic sink
  (fail-closed contract preserved, observability added).
- **#2346** — **BLOCKER (a11y):** conditional-breakpoint / logpoint text entry used `window.prompt()`
  (WCAG 2.2 AA non-compliant, the exact anti-pattern the codebase already replaced elsewhere);
  replaced with the repo's accessible focus-trapped dialog. Also fixed a `role="alert"` duplicate
  live region, a `stopping`-state status-bar mislabel ("Debug starting"), a missing setVariable
  side-effect disclosure, and same-file reveal routing through the heavy window-mutation path.
- **#2347** — **BLOCKER:** `revocationRequired()` killed a live debug session on _any_ unrelated M7
  settings mutation (a bare revision-counter bump). Fixed to only revoke on a real
  narrowing/deactivation. Also fixed a per-second watchdog overwriting real deactivation evidence
  with a colliding no-op record, added idle-tracked-workspace eviction, and wired the dedicated
  activation routes into the settings UI (they were dead production code — the UI only ever called
  the generic PATCH path).
- **#2348** — replaced a vacuous adversarial-bypass test (asserted a constant, not the behavior) with
  a real cross-stack rejection test; corrected stale performance numbers in the closeout evidence
  docs; routed DAP background-runtime failures through the redacted diagnostic sink.

**Production-readiness sweep:**

- **Security:** the live-evidence-projection failure path was silently swallowed in the production
  composition root; wired it to the diagnostic sink.
- **Performance:** **BLOCKER** — the per-second activation watchdog ran a full synchronous recursive
  `readdir`+`stat` walk of the operator runtime closure every tick per workspace (only file-content
  hashing had been cached); added an mtime-keyed walk cache. **MAJOR** — the shared LSP/DAP frame
  codec re-coalesced the whole buffer per extracted frame (O(frames×bytes)); fixed to coalesce once
  per batch with zero-copy slicing.
- **Maintainability:** the shared executable-resolution hardening primitive had silently swapped an
  OS-permission-aware `accessSync(X_OK)` check for a raw mode-bit test (a behavior change affecting
  both LSP and DAP preflight); restored the permission-aware check. Moved a test-only topology
  module into the `testing/` subtree.

**Mutation coverage:** the audit's own added diagnostic code left four survivors in
`dapProductionService.ts` (unasserted `operation`/`correlationId` fields); strengthened the
assertions and verified the kills by manual mutation.

## Reverted over-reach

The performance sweep hardened `scripts/check-perf-evidence.mjs` to enforce the full ADR-0136 D12
baseline-comparison addendum (baseline commit, repetition/run counts, alternating run order,
B4/B6 regression deltas, B6 raw samples, B11 growth) **without** updating the evidence _generator_
(`tests/e2e/editor-performance.spec.ts`) that must emit those fields. As shipped, this would have
failed the `check:perf-evidence` CI gate against freshly-generated Linux evidence on every
push-to-dev — a self-inflicted, un-passable gate. Reverted the checker to its `dev` baseline (the
genuine budget-ceiling and freshness protections are unchanged). The D12 baseline-comparison
addendum remains an unimplemented follow-up, documented below — it was never implemented in the
shipped epic (the evidence docs self-describe as "verification in progress").

## Verification

- `npm run codex:pre-pr` — full local gate chain green (typecheck, lint, format, ui typecheck/lint,
  21.8k unit tests, coverage ratchets, LCOV mapping, arch + negative-arch, ADR index, dependency
  hygiene, clean build, UI build, package-surface, editor bundle size, Chromium smoke). The two
  Linux-authoritative steps (`editor-release-evidence`, `editor-debugging-2348` E2E) are skipped on
  macOS by design and run in required CI.
- Debug-launch security mutation suite (`stryker.debug-launch.security.conf.json`, non-merge-blocking
  scheduled gate): the four survivors introduced by this change are killed; the remaining survivors
  are pre-existing (four provably-equivalent `code !== undefined` defensive-guard mutants + a small
  set of pre-existing coverage gaps), i.e. the epic's already-documented, still-open mutation
  closeout — not regressed by this change.

## Residual risks / follow-ups (not merge-blocking)

- **ADR-0136 D12 perf baseline-comparison is unimplemented** in `editor-performance.spec.ts` (single
  candidate run, no baseline delta, flat B11 probe). Pre-existing; needs a Linux+Playwright harness
  build-out. Not fixable or validatable in this non-browser environment.
- **Debug-launch mutation closeout** (pre-existing equivalent-guard + coverage-gap survivors) remains
  open on the scheduled, non-PR gate, exactly as the epic documented.
- `docs/release/1209-perf-evidence.json` is regenerated and stamped fresh by required CI on
  push-to-dev; the committed copy shows a local-checkout freshness mismatch only.

## Update impact

- Reuse/No-Duplication: every fix extends an existing subsystem (command-runner catalog, diagnostic
  sink, accessible-dialog pattern, glyph-margin lanes, M7 settings client). No parallel subsystem
  added; two dead/duplicate surfaces removed (unwired activation routes, no-op Layer-1 check).
- No trust boundary, evidence redaction, or quality gate was weakened to pass.

items.title: Production hardening: security, correctness, API, tests, and docs
items.body:
## Summary

Full production hardening pass addressing 70 findings from a multi-agent security and quality audit. Every finding has been fixed, tested with the race detector, and documented.

### Security & Correctness (Critical/High)
- **CoW spurious copy** (PROD-020) — `HandleWrite` now guards against processes not registered as sharers, eliminating potential memory corruption on concurrent fork/write
- **`PageTable.Clone` torn read** (PROD-039) — all per-page fields snapshotted under `page.LockShared()` in a single critical section; concurrent eviction can no longer produce an inconsistent clone
- **`MakeShared` race window** (PROD-040) — `Shared` and `ReadOnly` set atomically under `page.mu`; `Access()` can no longer observe `Shared=true, ReadOnly=false`
- **Cluster key collision** (PROD-043) — `PageClusterManager` key changed from bare `anchorPage uint64` to `processID+"\x00"+anchorPage`; different processes sharing the same anchor virtual page no longer collide
- **NRU TOCTOU** (PROD-060) — `accessCount` moved from `atomic.Int64` (accessed lock-free in `OnPageAccess`) to plain `int64` always under `mu`, closing the race with `SelectVictim`
- **Lock order deadlock** (PROD-045) — `parent.AddChild` moved outside `pm.mu.Lock()` to maintain `pm.mu → parent.mu` ordering

### Data Integrity
- **Compressed-page data loss** (PROD-016) — `DecompressPage` deletes the entry before frame allocation; `RestoreCompressed` is now called on OOM to put the entry back. `RestoreCompressed` stats corrected (no longer double-counts `pagesCompressed`)
- **PFF resident overflow** (PROD-015) — `adjustResidentSize` third branch clamps at `maxResident`
- **NUMA pointer leak** (PROD-055) — `GetNode` returns a struct copy, not a raw pointer

### API & Serialization
- **processJSON DTO** (PROD-046) — `HandleGetProcess`, `HandleCreateProcess`, `HandleForkProcess` serialize through `marshalProcess`, so all atomic fields appear as proper JSON numbers
- **`dropped_events` metric** (PROD-058) — new counter in `Metrics`; incremented in `emitEvent` when channel is full; included in `MetricsSnapshot` and reset in `Reset()`
- **`json:"-"` on atomic fields** (PROD-063) — prevents accidental direct serialization of `atomic.Bool`/`Int32`/`Int64` raw struct internals in `Frame`, `Page`, and `Process`

### Reliability
- **OOM prefetch** (PROD-057) — `updateWorkingSet` avoids per-call map allocation; `enforcePFFResident` removes victim from local slice instead of re-querying `GetUsedFrames` each iteration
- **CLI resource leak** (PROD-068) — `runComparison` and `runFramesSweep` use `defer mm0.Close()` instead of closing before the simulation runs
- **Trace file permissions** (PROD-067) — `Trace.Save` writes `0600` (was `0644`)
- **`ReplayTrace` nil guard** (PROD-050) — returns error on nil input; spurious `s.sleep()` removed

### Frontend
- **Scenario description bug** (PROD-030) — `app.js` captures `.scenario-desc` text before `textContent = 'Running...'` destroys child nodes; `finally` block uses the saved value

### Tests
- `defer mm.Close()` on all 18 integration tests and 7 benchmarks (PROD-035/069)
- `TestConcurrentForkAndAccess` uses `t.Errorf` for fork failures and adds correctness assertions (PROD-037)
- New `tests/unit/prefetch_e2e_test.go`: full pipeline test (sequential detect → cluster → prefetch → fault reduction) and cross-process isolation regression guard
- New `tests/unit/restore_compressed_test.go`: data-loss prevention, stats consistency, idempotence, and OOM-pressure scenario for `RestoreCompressed`

### Documentation
- README rewritten: all 12 algorithms documented, complete API reference, correct architecture diagram, accurate performance numbers, full test structure (was listing implemented features as "future enhancements")
- CHANGELOG: new `[Unreleased — Production Hardening]` section with every PROD-* fix categorized

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -race ./...` — all pass, no data races
- [x] `go test -race -count=5 -run "TestConcurrent|TestStress|TestCoW"` — stable across 5 runs
- [x] `go test -race -bench=. ./tests/benchmark/` — all benchmarks pass under race detector
- [x] `go vet ./...` — clean

items.title: ci(release): harden the two flakes that broke v0.1.1-canary.1
items.body:
`v0.1.1-canary.1` shipped, but only after two transient failures that each needed a manual re-run. Both passed on a plain re-run **with no code change**, so neither was a code defect — but a release that depends on someone noticing and re-running it will eventually ship late.

## 1. `hdiutil: create failed - Resource busy` (x64 Performance)

electrobun images the app with `hdiutil create -srcfolder .dmg-staging`. Spotlight is still crawling that tree — ~400 MB of freshly-written CEF — when the imaging engine starts walking it.

**Fix:** disable Spotlight indexing on the runner before the build.

Worth being precise about *why*, because the obvious explanation is wrong: the temp volume `hdiutil` mounts is `noowners,nobrowse`, and macOS **never indexes it** (measured — `mdutil -s` on that volume reports `Indexing disabled.` even with Spotlight fully on). The contention is on the **staging** side, on `/System/Volumes/Data`, where `.dmg-staging` lives and where `mds_stores` genuinely does crawl. `sudo mdutil -a -i off` covers exactly that volume.

This is a **mitigation, not a proof**: it removes the one contender we can observe. It is `|| true`-guarded and cannot fail the job.

## 2. `gh release view` transient failure → HTTP 422

This one was transient in cause but **deterministic in consequence**. The rolling feed releases (`updates` / `updates-performance`) *always* exist after the first release, so a flaky existence check falls through to `gh release create`, which dies on `HTTP 422: Release.tag_name already exists` — and takes the entire release with it.

**Fix:** `publish_feed()` forgives a failed `create` only when a re-check proves the release really does exist. A genuine create failure still fails the job.

Verified with stubbed-`gh` reproductions under `bash -e`:

| scenario | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| view flakes, release exists | 422 → **release dies** | re-check forgives → uploads → exit 0 |
| create genuinely fails | exit 1 | exit 1 (**still fails — not swallowed**) |

### Why the versioned-release step keeps the unguarded pattern

Deliberate, and commented in place so nobody "unifies" them. The exposure is inverted: a feed release *always* exists, so one flaky `view` there is fatal on every run. A versioned release does **not** exist yet on a tag push, so a flaky `view` lands in the `create` branch it was headed for anyway — the normal path is flake-immune. Only "re-run of a tag whose release already exists" **and** "a transient failure in that same run" can 422 there, and it fails closed (feeds already published, nothing corrupted, a re-run fixes it). Guarding it would be dead weight.

## 3. Size numbers

Corrected the Performance download to **~130 MB** (measured: 126 MB arm64, 135 MB x64) across both READMEs and the release notes; the smoke-test comment now says `~120 MB` for the *compressed payload*, which is a different number from the DMG and was being conflated.

## Also done outside this PR

Deleted the empty `v0.1.1-canary.0` tag (it died in the `vite build` OOM and had no release behind it).

items.title: fix(performance): bound the tiered cache blend, add vSAN OSA and Nutanix fast-tier models
items.body:
Closes #89 and #111.

Two changes that move numbers in **opposite** directions. They are together because the second was found by doing the first.

## #111 — the cache blend was a weighted average of capacities (correctness fix, numbers drop)

`src/engines/performance/index.ts`'s S2D tiered branch computed:

```ts
readCapIOPS = ws * (cacheCount * cacheIOPS) + (1 - ws) * (capCount * capIOPS)
```

That is a weighted average of two *capacities*, not the throughput of a system where a fixed fraction of requests must be served by each tier. If fraction `ws` of reads hit the cache and `1 - ws` must come from the capacity tier, the total `T` must satisfy **both** constraints at once:

```
ws · T ≤ C_cache   and   (1 - ws) · T ≤ C_cap
⟹  T = min( C_cache / ws , C_cap / (1 - ws) )
```

The slow path caps everything. The old formula let the fast tier's capacity leak into the total in proportion to how *little* traffic it served — so the faster the cache, the more absurd the result.

**Tiered S2D, `workingSetPercent = 20`: 318,914 → 7,136 IOPS.** A factor of 45. The old figure was unachievable on the hardware, and it has been in released output since the S2D model was introduced.

Nutanix's new write blend had the identical shape and was fixed the same way. Both now call one shared `boundedTierThroughput(shareA, capA, capB)` helper, so they cannot drift apart — which was the point of having vSAN reuse S2D's model in the first place.

## #89 — vSAN OSA and Nutanix get fast-tier models (new capability, numbers rise)

Previously only S2D's fast tier contributed anything; every other tiered platform was priced as if its SSDs were absent.

- **vSAN OSA** — reuses the (now correct) blend, gated on `diskGroupMode`. Writes are absorbed by the cache tier in **both** modes; reads blend by `workingSetPercent` **only in hybrid**, because all-flash dedicates 100% of the cache device to the write buffer and keeps no read cache.
- **Nutanix hybrid** — write-only, split by `randomPercent`, deliberately **not** the S2D blend: Nutanix routes writes above 1.5 MB straight past the OpLog to the extent store. Reads get no model — ILM promotion is touch-count triggered with no published hit rate to anchor a working-set split.
- **Ceph and BeeGFS — no model, with the specific reason in the code.** Ceph's WAL/DB never serves data reads; a BeeGFS metadata target cannot serve bulk data I/O at all. These replace a generic "not modelled" comment so the question stays settled.

Dispatch is `FAST_TIER_MODEL_BY_TOPOLOGY`, mirroring `NETWORK_MODEL_BY_TOPOLOGY`. A fifth platform is a table entry, not another orchestrator branch.

## Vectors (70/30 read/write)

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| **Tiered S2D** (bug fix) | 318,914 IOPS / 19,932 MB/s | **7,136 IOPS / 446 MB/s** |
| vSAN OSA hybrid | 2,585 / 162 | 7,136 / 446 |
| vSAN OSA all-flash | 2,585 / 162 | 4,771 / 298 (writes only; reads unchanged) |
| Nutanix, `randomPercent=100` | 2,585 / 162 | 4,771 / 298 |
| Nutanix, `randomPercent=5` | 2,903 / 4,677 | 2,961 / 4,732 |
| Ceph tiered | 2,100 / 131 | unchanged |
| BeeGFS tiered | 1,344 / 84 | unchanged |

## The test gap this exposed, and closed

The 45× error passed the **entire existing suite** — every S2D and vSAN assertion used relational bounds (`toBeGreaterThan`), so 1,391 tests were identically green with the wrong formula and the right one.

Added 8 tests that would have caught it: a pinned tiered-S2D vector, seven direct unit tests of `boundedTierThroughput` (both degenerate ends, cache-limited side, capacity-limited side, the crossover, and a `fast-check` property that the result never exceeds either single-tier bound). **Verified falsifiable** by temporarily restoring the weighted sum — 6 of 8 failed; the 2 that passed are the `shareA = 0` / `shareA = 1` ends where both formulas coincide, which is correct.

```
× the classic sanity check from #111: expected 500500 to be close to 2000
× pinned vector: bounded read IOPS/bandwidth: expected 361920 to be close to 3000
× property: Counterexample: [0.001, 2.002001001001119, 1]
```

Suite green: 72 files, 1402 tests.

Known and tracked separately as **#112**: write-back absorption still has no drain-rate ceiling, so sustained write throughput is overstated once a real cache saturates. Deliberately out of scope here.

Research: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-04-fast-tier-performance-research.md`.

items.body: Coauthor: @yctseng0211 @bingxche @michaelzhang-ai Summary Adds an AMD MI355X 2-node 1P1D disaggregation nightly benchmark covering all four DeepSeek-V4 models (Flash / Pro × FP8 / FP4), each running a GSM8K accuracy hard-gate before the perf sweep, built on top of the existing matrix / result-processing / summary layer with a new sglang-native launcher. - Four configs in scripts/ci/slurm/nightly-configs.yaml (dsv4{flash,pro}-{fp8,fp4}-mi355x-sglang, runner: mi355x), each backed by a per-model recipe under scripts/ci/slurm/recipes/mi355x-{fp8,fp4}/{dsv4flash,dsv4pro}/1k1k/1p1d.yaml. The full matrix runs every model on each nightly (strategy.matrix, fail-fast: false), so the models are fully independent and one failure never blocks the others. - GSM8K accuracy gate: each recipe carries a bench.accuracy section (full GSM8K, 8-shot, threshold 0.91). The launcher runs sglang.test.few_shot_gsm8k through the PD/LB path and gates on correctness before the perf sweep — performance numbers are only trusted once accuracy passes. - scripts/ci/slurm/launch_mi355x.sh: a self-contained Docker harness that sallocs two MI355X nodes and runs prefill + decode over MORI, a standalone load balancer, the GSM8K gate, then an sglang.bench_serving concurrency sweep — normalizing output into the process_result.py schema. FP4 vs FP8 is precision-driven (SGLANG_DSV4_FP4_EXPERTS), and weights resolve from the shared /it-share HF cache via refs/main, so the live snapshot is always picked up with no hardcoded hash. - New workflow .github/workflows/nightly-amd-mi355x-disagg.yml, on the self-hosted linux-sglang-mi35x-di runner. A setup job auto-resolves the latest published MI35x ROCm 7.2 + 7.0 image from Docker Hub each night (three-tier: workflow_dispatch input → auto-latest → recipe runtime.image), so the nightly always tracks the freshest build. Motivation Brings full nightly coverage of all four DeepSeek-V4 (Flash/Pro, FP8/FP4) 2-node 1P1D PD-disaggregation runs to AMD MI355X, with correctness gated before performance so regressions surface immediately. The design is intentionally sglang-native and self-contained: a self-hosted runner on the amd-sglang login node sallocs two nodes and drives the Docker harness over MORI directly. This keeps the pipeline lightweight and easy to maintain — it runs end-to-end with just sglang and Slurm, and slots cleanly into the existing nightly framework. --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :white_check_mark: [Run #28208677112](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/28208677112) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #28208677068](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/28208677068)

items.title: Productionize BAF fraud detection: orchestration, temporal split, drift loop
items.body:
## Summary

Brings the fraud-detection system from a working prototype to a production-shaped MLOps reference implementation. Adds retraining orchestration, closes the drift monitoring loop, and hardens the training methodology, on top of the reproducible training, hardened serving, and CI already in place. The full stack runs locally via docker compose at zero cloud cost.

## What's included

**Retraining orchestration (Airflow DAGs)**
- `fraud_drift_check` (daily): runs the Evidently drift check and triggers retraining when the drifted-column share crosses threshold.
- `fraud_retrain` (quarterly, plus drift-triggered): retrains, runs the evaluation gate, and promotes `@champion` only if the candidate passes.
- Drift logic relocated into the installed package (`fraud_detection.monitoring.drift`) so Airflow imports it cleanly; the CLI entrypoint is kept as a thin wrapper.
- DAG contracts guarded by dependency-free AST tests (Airflow is not a test dependency).

**Training methodology: temporal split**
- Replaced the random train/test split with a temporal one (train on the earliest months, evaluate on the most recent held-out months), mirroring production and preventing future-month leakage.
- Dropped `month` from the model's inputs; it now serves only as the split key and drift axis. Metrics held (about 0.55 recall and 0.89 ROC-AUC at the 5 percent FPR operating point), confirming `month` carried no generalizing signal.

**Closed the drift loop: live-traffic capture**
- The serving API now appends every scored `/predict` payload to a rolling `current.parquet` (bounded window, atomic writes, thread-safe, best-effort so telemetry never breaks scoring).
- This is the file the drift job compares against the frozen training reference, so drift is measured on real received traffic and is decoupled from how it was generated.

**Docs and hygiene**
- README updated: temporal-split rationale, closed drift loop, corrected dataset description (BAF is synthetic), accurate performance numbers.
- Generated Evidently reports are now gitignored.

## Testing
- 36 unit and integration tests pass; ruff lint and format clean.
- Full training pipeline verified end to end on BAF Base.csv; the producer/consumer contract between traffic capture and the drift job verified.

## What's next
- Phase 9: a realistic traffic simulator that replays the BAF benchmark's own temporal and cross-variant shifts through the live API, plus endpoint load testing.

## Notes
Portfolio reference implementation. Runs locally at zero cloud cost while preserving a topology that maps onto managed cloud services (S3, managed Postgres, tracking server, container runtime).

items.title: Document SSE flush regression and post-fix re-run plan
items.body:
## Summary

This PR documents a critical SSE flush regression (commit c70f0c1) that inflated baseline latencies by ~3.3x, invalidating benchmark results from Instance 5 (bb20555) and Instance 6 (c219fbd). The fix (08ba984) has been merged. This documentation update marks invalid data, preserves valid reference results from Instance 3, and provides a detailed re-run plan for post-fix validation.

## Key Changes

- **Added data validity notice** at the top of the benchmark guide explaining the regression, its impact, and which data is invalid
- **Marked invalid benchmark tables** with strikethrough formatting and explanatory notes for Instance 5-6 results (bb20555, c219fbd)
- **Elevated Instance 3 results** (Feb 10-14, pre-regression) as the current valid reference dataset with corrected performance numbers:
  - 13B P99 improvements: -79% to -85% (vs previously reported -24% to -51%)
  - Cache hit rates: 97-98% (vs 87-89%)
  - Throughput gains: +14% to +22% (vs +3% to +14%)
- **Added comprehensive Post-Fix Re-Run Plan** section with:
  - 16 prioritized test configurations across 4 priority tiers
  - Detailed command templates with environment variables
  - Expected outcomes and key questions for each tier
  - Results table template for tracking completion
- **Created MEMORY.md** for persistent cross-session context:
  - Root cause analysis of the SSE flush regression
  - Fix validation metrics (3.3x baseline improvement)
  - List of invalid vs valid benchmark instances
  - Post-fix results from Feb 27-28 validation runs (b63c165)
  - Architecture notes on tokenization overhead (8ms → 16ms regression)
  - Key commit reference table
- **Updated kv-cache-prefix-routing-benchmark.md** with validated 30-minute run results (b63c165)
- **Updated BACKLOG.md** with new optimization item for partial tokenization

## Notable Implementation Details

- The regression root cause: commit c70f0c1 changed `stream_backend_response()` to flush SSE only on first/last chunk instead of every chunk, causing intermediate tokens to buffer in Seastar's output_stream (8KB default)
- Fix (08ba984) restored per-chunk flush behavior
- Post-fix quick validation (13B 20u 1m) showed P99 -67.6% converging to -79.6% on full 10m run, matching Instance 3 (-78.7%)
- Identified secondary issue: tokenization overhead doubled from ~8ms to ~16.5ms due to thread pool + message boundary detection (commits 973768d, 3841bb7, 1a414c0)
- Run-to-run variance observed on main (P99 -79.6% vs +34.3% back-to-back), attributed to batched route learning's 10ms flush interval creating cross-shard routing divergence windows

## Files Modified

- `docs/benchmarks/benchmark-guide-8xA100.md` — Primary documentation update with validity notices and re-run plan
- `MEMORY.md` — New file for persistent context
- `docs/benchmarks/kv-cache-prefix-routing-benchmark.md` — Updated with validated results
- `BACKLOG.md` — Added tokenization optimization item

items.title: perf(ci): accelerate root quality gate
items.body:
## Summary

The root quality gate now completes the same research checks without resolving duplicate ephemeral environments or downloading CUDA-only packages on CPU runners. One locked Python 3.12 quality environment supplies pytest, the scientific/PDF stack, Ruff, and ty; Linux Torch resolves from an explicit CPU index, and CI reuses the lock-keyed uv cache.

Pytest now attacks the measured bottleneck with bounded `loadscope` distribution, at most four workers, and one native math thread per worker. Local execution stays serial unless explicitly opted into parallelism, and the canonical `python3 scripts/run_quality_checks.py` entry point is unchanged. The only test that wrote tracked PDF artifacts now redirects every output to its temporary directory before parallel execution.

| Measurement | PR #357 baseline | This branch |
|---|---:|---:|
| Full quality gate | 9m00s on GitHub Actions | 2m19.80s locally |
| Pytest phase | 489.83s | 133.66s |
| Inventory | 492 passed, 3 skipped, 54 subtests | 496 passed, 3 skipped, 54 subtests |

The local numbers establish a strong correctness/performance signal, but the acceptance benchmark remains the hosted Linux check: the first new-lock run and an immediate same-commit rerun must each finish within five minutes.

## Validation

- `QUALITY_PYTEST_WORKERS=auto python3 scripts/run_quality_checks.py` — 496 passed, 3 skipped, 54 subtests; every validator, provenance, Ruff, and ty passed in 2m19.80s.
- Linux/Python 3.12 locked resolution — `torch 2.13.0+cpu`; no NVIDIA or Triton packages.
- Targeted four-worker collision stress set — 43 passed, 2 skipped in 50.81s; tracked publication outputs remained unchanged.
- Review-fix checks — focused wrapper/PDF tests, full Ruff, full ty, provenance freshness, and `git diff --check` passed.

## Related

Related: #360

## New concepts

### Locked quality dependency groups

A PEP 735 dependency group gives tooling dependencies their own declared surface without pretending the repository is one installable application. Here, `quality` is locked once and shared by every root gate, while experiment-specific and Modal environments remain independent.

The explicit PyTorch CPU index is package-scoped: Torch comes from the CPU wheel repository, while NumPy and the rest continue to resolve from PyPI. This prevents an alternate package index from accidentally becoming a global source.

Use this pattern for a stable multi-tool environment. Keep ephemeral `uvx` execution for genuinely isolated one-off tools whose dependency graph should not become part of the root contract.

### Scope-aware test parallelism

`pytest-xdist --dist loadscope` groups module functions and test classes so expensive scoped fixtures are not needlessly recreated across workers. A fixed upper worker bound and one native math thread per worker prevent xdist plus NumPy/Torch internals from multiplying CPU contention.

The scheduler does not make shared filesystem writes safe. Tests that build artifacts must still redirect outputs to per-test temporary paths, as the PDF regression test now does.

Use scope-aware distribution when a suite has enough independent modules/classes to amortize worker startup. Prefer serial execution for small suites or tests whose shared external state cannot be isolated.

---

items.title: Add the warp-per-chunk LZ4 decode kernel

milestone.title: M1 - LZ4 block
milestone.description: Warp-cooperative LZ4 block decode, fuzz-diffed against liblz4, first honest numbers

items.body:
# What & why

M1 ladder step 3 (masterplan section 9): the LZ4 block decoder behind the frozen batch ABI, replacing the stub. This is the fail-closed heart on the GPU - the project's login path. Closes #14.

One warp per chunk over a grid-stride loop; all 32 lanes run the merged validation ladder (`src/lz4_block.h`, merged in #17) redundantly in lockstep and fan out by lane for every copy; overlapping matches use the closed-form modular gather that reads only the region finalized before the match; `__syncwarp()` carries the intra-warp memory ordering at the two copy boundaries; zero shared memory, no table, no dispatch heuristic.

## Type of change

- [x] Decode kernel / device code
- [x] Format support (LZ4 / Snappy / GDeflate / Zstd)
- [ ] API surface
- [ ] Performance
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] Refactor / code quality
- [ ] Build / CI / supply chain
- [ ] Docs

## Engineering checklist

- [x] Fail-closed preserved: the kernel runs the already-hardened parser ladder; every device read/write is bounded by what the parser guarantees; a rejected chunk reports bytes_written 0 and never presents its partial dst as valid (now asserted in the test).
- [x] Oracle coverage: pristine pairs decode byte-exact; the mutant corpus is held to the two-direction oracle-parity contract on the GPU decoder, matching the CPU twin including the single offset==0 stricter case.
- [x] Determinism preserved: same-batch-twice bit-identical across the whole Silesia corpus and the fixture batch.
- [x] Every CUDA API call's error is checked (host launch: drain + post-launch check); no exceptions cross the ABI.
- [x] Adversarial review was run (security-review gated) - see Notes.

## Performance checklist

Minimal-correct kernel; numbers are #15's job (the bench GPU path). Recorded here per the masterplan occupancy plan: 46 registers/thread, so >= 32 warps/SM is achievable on sm_86. The per-element 64-bit modulo in the match gather is a known perf-pass (#16) target, not a correctness issue.

- [ ] The claim is measured: deferred to #15.
- [ ] No regression against baseline: n/a (first GPU decode; baseline is the CPU oracle in docs/BENCHMARKS.md).

## Quality checklist

- [x] Minimal: no shared memory, no sequence table, no dispatch heuristic - the least kernel that is correct and fail-closed.
- [x] Self-documenting: the closed-form gather, the two syncwarp barriers, the offset==0/modulo-by-zero link, the no-__restrict__ invariant on dst, and the cap-tied index math each carry their why.
- [x] Conformance tests pass; the new structural properties (real decode, failure contract, grid-stride coverage) are locked into gpu_fixture.

## Verification

- [x] `cmake --build` - both configurations clean under warnings-as-errors.
- [x] `ctest` - 7/7 on the RTX 3080.
- [x] **Whole-Silesia GPU-vs-oracle diff: 3239 chunks, 211.94 MB, 0 byte mismatches, 0 nondeterministic** across a second run.
- [x] gpu_fixture: 12 pairs byte-exact + 310 mutants two-direction parity (248 oracle-rejected, 1 offset==0 stricter, identity-pinned) + 40000-chunk grid-stride wraparound; failure contract + poison intact.
- [x] CI-parity run without a GPU: green, all identity pins.
- [x] Prettier - clean.
- [x] Docs: cudec.h result-contract comment updated; masterplan section 9 already specifies this kernel.

## Notes

Security-review gated (decoder validation is the login path). Three lenses:

- **CUDA domain: PASS.** Confirmed the central question - `__syncwarp()` is sufficient for the cross-lane global-memory ordering the kernel relies on (both the documented CUDA memory model and the on-target gates agree; a `__threadfence_block` is not needed). Verified the two barriers are necessary and sufficient, the warp-uniform indexing eliminates partial-warp `__syncwarp` UB by construction, the closed-form gather equals sequential LZ4 for every offset >= 1, and no OOB / div-by-zero / result-store race exists.
- **Correctness + robustness: NEEDS_IMPROVEMENT -> all fixed.** The kernel was ruled analytically sound; the five findings were verification-net gaps (per the project's "verify empirically, not by reasoning" invariant): (1) the failure-contract `bytes_written==0` on a kernel reject was untested - a broken kernel setting it unconditionally would have passed; (2) the grid-stride multi-chunk-per-warp path had zero empirical coverage (needs > 32768 chunks); (3) `stricter_count==1` pinned the count but not the identity; (4) the poison check was vacuous on pristine pairs; (5) stale comments. All five closed - the failure contract is now asserted, a 40000-chunk test forces the wraparound and proves exactly-once, the stricter case is pinned by identity to the offset==0 mutant, pristine pairs carry slack capacity, comments corrected. A closure pass re-verified all five PASS. No declined findings.

**Toolchain constraint (documented):** compute-sanitizer memcheck/racecheck cannot run in the container - the WSL2/WDDM GPU passthrough aborts the tool at init ("Device not supported"), an environment block rather than a code result. The whole-corpus GPU-vs-oracle byte diff (an OOB corrupts output) plus same-batch-twice determinism (a race breaks it) are the standing substitute gates; run the real sanitizer when a Linux-native GPU or the debugger interface is available.

items.title: Fix invisible "Your Progress" dashboard chart
items.body:
## Problem
The dashboard's **Your Progress** area chart rendered empty — axes and the Total/Avg stats showed correct numbers, but no line/area appeared, even though `/dashboard/performance/` returned valid data.

## Root cause
The theme defines `--primary` as a **complete color**:
```css
--primary: hsl(225.7181 51.8948% 50.4104%);
```
but the chart wrapped it again:
```tsx
stroke="hsl(var(--primary))"   // → hsl(hsl(225…%)) → invalid color
```
`hsl(hsl(...))` is not a valid CSS color, so the area's stroke and gradient fill resolved to transparent. The data and axes were fine — only the series was invisible.

## Fix — `components/dashboard/task_completion_graph.tsx`
- Use `var(--primary)` directly (stroke + both gradient stops).
- Fix the X-axis `interval`: it was set for daily data (`7/15/30`), which collapsed the **monthly** payload to a single tick (only "Apr 1" showed). Now `interval={0}` with `minTickGap` so every month renders.

## Verification
Confirmed live: with the fix, the area renders the completion trend and the X-axis shows each month. `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## Note (not changed here)
The same `hsl(var(--…))` antipattern exists in `components/ui/sidebar.tsx` and `components/company/employee_card.tsx` (subtle shadows/gradients) — harmless visually but worth a follow-up sweep since the theme uses full color values.

items.title: fix: lower x86 baseline to x86-64-v2 so pre-AVX2 CPUs reach the scalar fallback (#137)
items.body:
Implements the maintainer-ruled fix direction (a) from #137: lower the global x86 compile baseline from `x86-64-v3` to `x86-64-v2` so the runtime dispatch and the #106 scalar fallback actually function on pre-AVX2 CPUs.

## Mechanism

`.cargo/config.toml` applied `-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3` to **all** plain (non-`#[target_feature]`) code. That includes `turbovec::search::search`'s dispatch closure — LUT setup, heap init, and the inlined `score_query_into_heap` scalar fallback — which runs **before** the `is_x86_feature_detected!` checks. At v3 that closure alone contained **523 above-v2 instructions (302 `%ymm` references)**, so a pre-Haswell / AVX2-hiding-VM CPU raises `#UD` → SIGILL before dispatch can ever choose the fallback: exactly the CPUs #106 exists to serve.

The fix keeps the hot paths dispatched because the four SIMD kernels (`search_multi_query_avx2`, `search_multi_query_avx512bw`, `avx2_batch_flush_to_fa`, `avx2_post_flush_heap_update` — `turbovec/src/search.rs:168,402,700,737`) are `#[target_feature]`-gated functions: they are compiled with their full feature sets **regardless of the baseline** (re-tuned by the baseline's tuning model — see Performance below) and selected at runtime. Non-kernel glue drops from v3 to v2 codegen. ARM/aarch64 builds are byte-identical in intent and config: the section is scoped `[target.'cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")']` and only the `target-cpu` value changed.

## Wheel pipeline findings

- `release-pypi.yml` builds all wheels via `maturin-action` with `working-directory: turbovec-python` inside the repo checkout and sets **no RUSTFLAGS of its own** — cargo walks up and applies the root `.cargo/config.toml`. So the shipped x86_64 Linux and Windows wheels inherited v3, and this one-line config change fixes them; no workflow edit needed.
- The published crates.io `.crate` does **not** contain `.cargo/config.toml` (per the #166 file list), so `cargo add turbovec` users were never affected; the CHANGELOG entries say so.

## Evidence 1 — disassembly audit (macOS ARM host, cross-compiled `x86_64-apple-darwin`, release)

Scripted audit of the emitted `.s` (`cargo rustc --release --target x86_64-apple-darwin -p turbovec --lib -- --emit asm`): attribute every instruction to its enclosing symbol; flag any `%ymm`/`%zmm` reference, VEX/EVEX `v*` mnemonic, or BMI1/BMI2/`lzcnt` scalar op (i.e. anything above x86-64-v2); allowlist only the four `#[target_feature]` kernels plus `pulp::x86::V3::vectorize::__impl` (pulp is faer's SIMD layer; its `__impl` is generated with `#[target_feature(enable = ...)]` per feature and the `V3` token is only constructible after runtime detection — the same dispatch pattern as our kernels, verified in pulp 0.18.22 source).

| build | above-v2 instructions outside gated code | violating symbols |
|---|---|---|
| `target-cpu=x86-64-v3` (old) | **6,576** | **200** (incl. `search::search` closure: 523) |
| `target-cpu=x86-64-v2` (new) | **0** | **0** |

The v2 binary still contains the full AVX kernels (audit counts inside allowlisted symbols: 1,098 AVX/AVX-512 instructions in `search_multi_query_avx512bw`, 537 in `search_multi_query_avx2`, 251 in `avx2_post_flush_heap_update`), i.e. lowering the baseline did not strip the dispatched kernels.

**Scope of the zero-claim:** this audit covers the `turbovec` crate's own codegen units (the crate's emitted `.s`). Adversarial review extended the same audit to the fully-linked binary and verified, family by family, that every above-v2 instruction contributed by dependency crates (~71k, dominated by pulp/faer) also lives in runtime-feature-gated code — and confirmed pulp's gating in both 0.18.22 and 0.21.5.

<details>
<summary>Audit script (local verification tooling, not committed)</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Audit an x86_64 .s file: flag AVX/AVX2/AVX-512/BMI/FMA (above-x86-64-v2)
instructions appearing OUTSIDE the #[target_feature]-gated kernel symbols."""
import re, sys, collections

ASM = sys.argv[1]
ALLOW = re.compile(
    r"search_multi_query_avx2|search_multi_query_avx512bw|"
    r"avx2_batch_flush_to_fa|avx2_post_flush_heap_update|"
    r"pulp3x86\dV\d+9vectorize6__impl"  # pulp runtime-gated vectorize impls
)
LEGACY_V = {"verr", "verw", "vmcall", "vmlaunch", "vmresume", "vmxoff",
            "vmxon", "vmclear", "vmptrld", "vmptrst", "vmread", "vmwrite",
            "vmfunc"}
BMI = re.compile(r"^\s+(mulxq?|pdepq?|pextq?|shlxq?|shrxq?|sarxq?|rorxq?|"
                 r"andnq?|andnl|bextrq?|blsiq?|blsmskq?|blsrq?|lzcntq?|lzcntl)\b")
VMNEM = re.compile(r"^\s+(v[a-z0-9]+)\b")
WIDE = re.compile(r"%[yz]mm\d+")

sym = None
bad = collections.defaultdict(list)
allowed_hits = collections.Counter()
label_re = re.compile(r"^(_?[A-Za-z_.$][\w.$]*):")

with open(ASM) as f:
    for n, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        m = label_re.match(line)
        if m and not m.group(1).startswith(("L", "l_", ".")):
            sym = m.group(1); continue
        hit = False
        if WIDE.search(line) and not line.lstrip().startswith((".", "#", "//")):
            hit = True
        else:
            vm = VMNEM.match(line)
            if vm and vm.group(1) not in LEGACY_V:
                hit = True
            elif BMI.match(line):
                hit = True
        if hit:
            if sym and ALLOW.search(sym):
                allowed_hits[sym] += 1
            else:
                bad[sym or "<no-symbol>"].append((n, line.rstrip()))

for s, c in allowed_hits.most_common():
    print(f"  {c:6d}  {s}")
if bad:
    print("VIOLATIONS outside gated kernels:")
    for s, lines in bad.items():
        print(f"  {s}: {len(lines)}")
    sys.exit(1)
print("PASS: no above-v2 instructions outside #[target_feature] kernels.")
```
</details>

## Evidence 2 — full suite under Rosetta 2 (executes the fallback end-to-end)

`cargo test --release --target x86_64-apple-darwin -p turbovec` on the ARM host runs every test binary under Rosetta 2, which reports **no** AVX/AVX2/FMA/BMI (probe: `sse4.2: true`, everything above: `false`) — a v2-class environment. Dispatch therefore takes the scalar-fallback branch (`search.rs:1577`) for every search in the suite.

**Result: 209/209 passed, 0 failed** (lib 30, concurrent_search 8, filtering 15, from_parts 33, id_map 19, input_validation 15, io_hardening 11, io_v4 13, io_versioning 9, kernel_correctness 7, lazy_init 24, rotation 5, state_sequences 9, swap_remove 6, tqplus_calibration 2, doc-tests 3).

**Honest limitation:** Rosetta cannot demonstrate the *SIGILL itself* — I verified directly that it executes VEX/AVX2 instructions it does not advertise (a `#[target_feature]` `_mm256_add_epi32` probe runs fine while `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")` returns false), and accordingly the old v3 build also happens to pass under Rosetta. So the Rosetta run proves "the scalar fallback genuinely executes end-to-end and returns correct results at the new baseline"; the SIGILL-on-real-silicon claim rests on the disassembly audit above — genuine pre-AVX2 CPUs raise `#UD` on VEX encodings by architecture definition, and the audit shows the v3 build put 6,576 of them in unconditionally-reachable code and the v2 build puts zero.

## AVX-capable machines still get the kernels

Both AVX kernels are present in the v2 binary (symbol + instruction counts above) and the dispatch logic is untouched — `avx512bw && avx512f` → AVX-512 kernel, else `avx2` → AVX2 kernel, else scalar. CI's `ubuntu-latest`/`windows-latest` runners are x86_64 **with** AVX2, so a green Rust CI on this PR is the execution proof that the AVX2 kernel path still selects and computes correctly at the v2 baseline (the same suite includes kernel-vs-scalar correctness comparisons).

## Performance

No benchmark numbers claimed. The gated kernels keep their full instruction-set capability, but they are **not bit-identical** across baselines: `target-cpu` also selects LLVM's tuning model, and measured deltas include `search_multi_query_avx512bw` growing 1,808 → 1,836 instructions at v2 (some unaligned 256-bit ops split into 128-bit pairs by the v2 tuning heuristics) and the AVX2 kernel being outlined at v2 where v3 had fully inlined it into the dispatch closure (that inlining being the bug itself). Correctness of both kernels at the new baseline is proven by CI (AVX2 runners) and the suite's kernel-vs-scalar comparisons; performance impact is expected to be minor but is unmeasured — **recommend one benchmark run on the x86 bench instance before the next release** to confirm. The other expected x86 delta is non-kernel glue (rotation loops, LUT build, heap bookkeeping outside the kernels) dropping from v3 to v2 codegen; if x86 CI timings visibly regress that should be investigated before merge. ARM builds are entirely outside the config section's scope and unaffected.

Closes #137

Awaiting maintainer review — do not merge.

Interpolating `someFragment.code` into another `mantleCode` template now splices the fragment's source into the highlighted output at build time, instead of treating it as an opaque runtime placeholder. - same-module `mantleCode` consts referenced as `.code` (declared before use)

items.title: Log the viewpoint-2 score mis-join
items.body:
Outcome of investigating the stale `fix_battle_order` branch. Records a live defect and the constraint it puts on the game migration. **No behavior change** — docs and tests only.

## The defect

`Game.score_object` finds a `GameScore` by matching the facade's direction against the row's, but a `BattleViewpoint` rewrites field *names* and not lookup *keys*. So from viewpoint 2 each game reads the other game's score row.

A second error hides it: `BattleViewpoint.game_scores_list` wraps each row in a `GameScoreViewpoint` carrying the battle-level viewpoint, which swaps similarities that are already stored in game order. Composed, the two name the right warrior in the wrong game — so battle score, performance and rating all come out correct, and the only wrong numbers on the site are the warrior-arena page's two per-game columns, each showing what belongs to the other one.

That cancellation is why this survived unnoticed since `a0c080b` replaced the `Battle.lcs_len_*` columns with `GameScore` rows: the old `map_field_name_x_x_x` flipped direction *and* warrior index in one place, and only the warrior-index half made it into the new shape — where it is wrong anyway, since `GameScore` stores in game order while the old columns stored in battle order.

## Why it matters to `docs/game-migration.md`

Step 2 hydrates each viewpoint from its game rows, which repairs the mis-join for free and leaves the swap inverting every viewpoint-2 battle score. The step's own claim that "the score-averaging semantics are unchanged" holds only if both go, so the ordering constraint is recorded with the plan rather than only in the registry.

The fix also clears the last reader selecting on `GameScore.direction` — the condition step 1 is waiting on.

## The tests

`test_game_reports_its_own_similarities` states the contract as a parametrized table. The viewpoint-1 rows pass and are a regression guard the code did not have; the viewpoint-2 rows are `xfail(strict=True)`, so a whole fix has to come back and remove the marker.

`test_battle_score_splits_between_viewpoints` pins the invariant that hides the defect. Verified against every variant of the fix:

| | symmetry test | rating tests |
|---|---|---|
| today | pass | pass |
| direction mapped only (what `fix_battle_order` does) | **fail** | **fail** |
| swap dropped only | **fail** | **fail** |
| both (whole fix) | pass | pass |

Under the whole fix the entire suite passes untouched and the two `xfail` rows go `XPASS(strict)` — which is what verifies the entry's claim that no values move and no rating changes, so the fix needs no sign-off.

## Deliberately not here

The fix itself. It is small — map the row selection and drop the swap, after which `GameScoreViewpoint` wraps nothing and its scoring properties move back onto `GameScore` — but it changes numbers on a public page and deserves its own reviewed commit. `TODO.md` carries it as the next move.

No repair command either: every `GameScore` row in the database is correct, and `verify_games` has nothing to find. The damage is entirely on the read path.

items.title: Read a game's score off the game it names
items.body:
Clears the gate that step 1 of `docs/game-migration.md` waits on: the viewpoint-2 score mis-join.

## The bug

Two errors that cancelled each other.

`Game.score_object` found a score row by matching a direction label, but a label is battle-relative while the facade asking for it is relative to its viewpoint — so from viewpoint 2 each game read *the other game's* score. Hiding that, `BattleViewpoint.game_scores_list` wrapped every row in a `GameScoreViewpoint` swap of similarities that were already stored in game order.

Composed, they put the right warrior's name on the wrong game's numbers. Battle scores, performance and ratings came out correct; only the warrior-arena page's two per-game columns were wrong, each showing what belonged to the other one.

## The fix

Both errors go in one change, because repairing either alone inverts every viewpoint-2 battle score:

- the lookup keys on the warrior going first, which identifies the game row, instead of on a direction label;
- `GameScoreViewpoint` is deleted rather than adjusted — its `score`, `score_rev` and `cooperation_score` move onto `GameScore`, whose fields are already in game order, so nothing rewrites them on the way out.

`GameScore.direction` is left with a single reader (the audit's re-derivation), which drops with the directional columns in step 2.

## Verification

**Battle-level scores are unchanged to the bit** — measured by stashing the change and re-probing the same fixture:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| viewpoint 1 battle score | `0.38095238095238093` | `0.38095238095238093` |
| viewpoint 2 battle score | `0.6190476190476191` | `0.6190476190476191` |
| viewpoint 2 `game_1_2` | `w1=0.2 w2=0.1` (wrong game, swapped) | `w1=0.4 w2=0.3` |
| viewpoint 2 `game_2_1` | `w1=0.3 w2=0.4` | `w1=0.1 w2=0.2` |

No rating moves. `warriors/` goes from 146 passed + 2 xfailed to 149 passed, 0 xfailed — the two `MIS_JOIN` cases now pass, and one test is new. `makemigrations --check` reports no schema change; flake8 and pylint are clean.

The unmerged `fix_battle_order` branch takes the half-fix path — it maps the direction through the viewpoint but keeps the swap. Running its approach against this fixture gives viewpoint 2 a battle score of `0.381`, i.e. viewpoint 1's score, so the pair no longer sums to 1 and every rating moves. That branch is superseded and can be deleted.

## Query cost

Selecting by the game row reaches `game_score.game`, so the two hot read paths (`WarriorArena.update_rating` and the warrior-arena page) prefetch `game_scores__game`. A test pins the query count against the *battle count* rather than against a number, so it survives unrelated query changes and still fails if a prefetch drops the game — verified failing at 10 vs 4 queries when the prefetch is removed.

## Also

Removes the resolved `TODO.md` entry and adds one for `GameScore.cooperation_score`, which has no test. Updates the now-stale references in `docs/game-migration.md`, `docs/battle-display.md` and `docs/data-model.md`.

One thing deliberately left alone: `Game` still has six near-identical properties that fetch `score_object`, None-check and delegate. Collapsing them is possible for the first time after this change, but `Game` is deleted wholesale in step 2, so it would be short-lived churn.

Three stacked pieces toward running and benchmarking the NF4 teacher vs the ternary student.

## 1 — ABI residency checks (`apple_installation.rs`)
`derive_nf4_tile640_arena_abi` now takes `arena_capacity` and proves the teacher's triplet is safe to bind: dtype-natural **alignment** (FP32 metadata ÷4), **bounds** (offset+len ≤ capacity, checked add), and pairwise **non-overlap** — not just matching lengths. Both call sites updated; **negative tests** cover every branch. (Per-slot 16 KB is the IOSurface *base* alignment, not the per-view requirement, so enforcing it would wrongly reject valid packed arenas.)

## 2 — distillation numeric core (`compilation::distill_core`)
Std-only, unit-tested: `kd_divergence` (T²·KL teacher→student), `top1_agreement`, `block_accept`. The metrics the block loop gates on. `kernels/DISTILL_RUNTIME.md` wires it to the existing `distill_worker`.

## 3 — truthful benchmark harness (new)
- **`compilation::bench_metrics`** (std-only, tested): perplexity, throughput stats (median/p90/p99), effective-bpw, teacher-vs-student `compare`.
- **`tools/nf4tile640_ref.rs`**: CPU NF4Tile640 dequant+GEMV reference using the real 16-entry NF4 codebook + the packer's exact byte/group convention. GEMV parity vs direct reference is exact; **NF4 reconstructs Gaussian weights at rel-L2 ≈ 0.13** vs the ternary student's **≈ 0.5** — the fidelity gap distillation must close, quantified.
- **`kernels/BENCHMARK.md`**: the fair protocol (same machine/prompts/greedy/warmup, median+tails; prefill & decode tok/s, TTFT, bpw, PPL, top-1 agreement, KL).

## Build / run reality (important)
- `compute-core` **does build on Linux** under `--features backend-cpu` (needs cmake+clang). But **running a `.cimage` forward needs a `metal::Device`** — so live inference (and the *performance* numbers) are **Mac-only**. Linux validates correctness/plumbing; the benchmark harness makes the Mac numbers truthful and comparable.
- **Verified on Linux:** `distill_core` (in-crate build + tests), `bench_metrics` (tests), `nf4tile640_ref` (parity + fidelity), and the ABI derivation logic (standalone replica: happy + fixtures + all negatives).
- **Author-only (your Mac):** `apple_installation` is gated to `mlx/prism-backend`; `mlx-backend` fails MLX's cmake configure on Linux (needs the MLX source checkout), so those edits + their tests compile on your Mac.

## Next
Capture teacher logits from the NF4 forward on the Mac and run the first real block through `distill_core` + `ternary_pipeline`, scoring with `bench_metrics`. Pushed file-by-file via the contents API; squash-merge recommended.

> 🤖 SPARQ agent [FABLE-5]

Closes the conformance-table clause of the comparative-benchmarking epic: a HONEST per-suite cross-engine **conformance pass-rate** consolidation — sparq's actual CI-enforced scoreboard floors vs peers' **PUBLISHED** W3C EARL / implementation-report results. Bead **sq-hmd7l.22** (epic sq-hmd7l).

New file: `research/gap-conformance-cross-engine-2026-07.md`. **Docs/research only — no `crates/` source, no bench run** (sparq's numbers are already measured in the scoreboard; peer numbers are their published reports).

## What it does

- **sparq column = the ACTUAL scoreboard**, verified on `origin/main`: every number is a floor const (`scoreboard::SUITES`, `floors::<lane>::FLOOR`, and the crate-local `*_FLOOR` consts the guard test pins), each cited to its source + the suite pin it was measured at. Reproduce with `cargo run --release -p sparq-conformance --bin sparq-conformance-scoreboard`.
- **Peer column = published EARL only**, each cell URL + retrieval-date cited (all retrieved 2026-07-10). A peer with no published per-suite number gets an explicit **NOT-PUBLISHED** cell — never a sparq win by omission.
- **Suite-version mismatches flagged per row** (e.g. sparq pins later json-ld-api HEADs with slightly larger denominators than the 10-Apr-2025 EARL report; the 2013 W3C SPARQL report is REC-era, pre-dating every modern engine).
- **Fixed verdict vocabulary** (CLEARLY-AHEAD / AHEAD-BUT-NOT-OOM / PARITY / BEHIND / NOT-MEASURED / NOT-COMPARABLE).

## Honest headline

The dominant finding is **NOT-COMPARABLE** for the SPARQL family: modern peers (Oxigraph, QLever, Comunica) publish a BINARY "compliant"/known-failure-list posture, not per-suite counts, and the only numeric multi-engine SPARQL dataset is the 2013 W3C report. sparq's fully-enumerated 1229-count is a transparency lead, **not** a measured pass-rate win — and the record says so.

Where a genuine same-suite comparison exists:

| Family | Verdict |
|---|---|
| SolidLab ODRL | **PARITY** — EXACT 67/68 match with the suite's own reference evaluator, identical suite + oracle (the one strictly-matched row) |
| SHACL core | **PARITY** — 98/98 == the full core partition; peers are 100% over core+SPARQL |
| JSON-LD 1.1 | **BEHIND** — expand 71.7% / frame 66.3% / compact 75.6% vs mature processors' 97–100% (honest gap; follow-up bead noted) |
| GeoSPARQL | **NOT-COMPARABLE** — published benchmark is requirements-weighted, not a test-count |
| SPARQL query/update/syntax, Protocol/GSP, RDF-syntax | **NOT-COMPARABLE** — no like-for-like published peer count |

items.body: Second step of the fast-engine lane: speed up the price-level index. Full gate green — 115 pytest tests, `test_system.py` smoke 4/4, black + flake8 + compileall clean. ## The change `PriceLevelManager` kept `sorted_ticks` ordered with a **Python linear-scan insert** and an O(n) `list.remove` on empty-level cleanup. This replaces both with `bisect` using a per-side key (buy descending, sell ascending), so the index lookup is a binary search instead of a Python loop. Best-first ordering is unchanged, so no other consumer (`get_best_price`, snapshots, `_can_fully_fill`) needed changes. `add_wide` (ns/op): 687,178 → **89,034** at n=5k; 3,484,626 → **1,569,972** at n=20k. ## Why `bisect`, not a sorted-container dependency `bisect` gives O(log n) *search* but `list` insert/remove is still an O(n) memmove, so this is a large constant-factor win rather than true O(log n). A real O(log n) structure (`sortedcontainers.SortedList`) only helps once a single book holds thousands of distinct price levels — unrealistic. Measured isolated index insert (random ticks): | Distinct levels | `bisect` + list ns/op | `SortedList` ns/op | | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 2,000 | 1,455 | 2,094 | | 5,000 | 2,177 | 2,428 | | 20,000 | 5,583 | 2,709 | | 50,000 | 11,856 | 2,766 | `bisect` + list is **faster** below the ~5k-level crossover (realistic books) and adds no dependency, so none was taken.
